title: Two missing pieces in the AI safety discussion
gist: Noah Smith argues the AI-doom wave triggered by Jacob Coxon's Anthropic resignation and Amodei's 'pace the frontier' call needs two things: a concrete kill path to convince skeptics (AI-designed bioweapons) and a way to get China to slow down (demonstration cyberattacks using China's own open-weight models to convince the CCP superintelligence threatens its rule).

insights.claim: Jacob Coxon's resignation from Anthropic, alleging OpenAI and Anthropic are racing to self-improving superintelligence, went mega-viral and pushed AI extinction risk into mainstream national news and politics in September 2026.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: AI risk has become a mass political issue, raising odds of regulatory intervention in frontier AI.
insights.quote: I resigned from Anthropic today. I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly.

insights.claim: Politicians are responding to the AI risk wave: Barack Obama is urging Democrats to focus on AI risk, Bernie Sanders is drafting a bill to ban AI superintelligence with 20-year prison sentences, and Trump is resisting calls for a slowdown though advisors reportedly push him to act.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Signals a non-trivial chance of legislative caps on frontier AI development that would hit AI capex and valuations.
insights.quote: Bernie Sanders is drafting a bill to ban AI “superintelligence”, including 20-year prison sentences for anyone working on the technology.

insights.claim: Grace et al. (2024) surveyed thousands of AI researchers; the median gave a 5-10% probability of extinction-level outcomes from AI and the average was 15-20%.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Shows elite insiders' risk estimates are large and long-standing, so the public catching up is a sentiment shift rather than new information.
insights.quote: The median AI researcher gave “doom” a 5-10% probability (depending on how the question was phrased), while their average probability was between 15% and 20%.

insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Capability shocks and visible AI-agent incidents are now the catalysts for policy and sentiment swings.

insights.claim: Dario Amodei published 'We Must Pace the Frontier', calling for a coordinated industry slowdown in AI capabilities, with Anthropic unilaterally committing to give third-party evaluators permanent employee-level access to its work.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A leading lab publicly arguing to slow capability growth is a direct signal on future model cadence and industry capex trajectory.

insights.claim: Elon Musk, Sam Altman and Demis Hassabis quickly endorsed Amodei's pacing call; Altman said OpenAI would also adopt independent evaluators with employee-like access, and some labs are reportedly holding secret talks on joint slowdown.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Coordinated slowdown among frontier labs would reshape competitive dynamics and possibly raise antitrust questions.

insights.claim: Amodei's stated reasons for heightened worry are the Hugging Face agent attack and the prospect of near-term recursive self-improvement (RSI) where AI improves itself without human help.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: RSI expectations are now driving policy positioning of the labs themselves.

insights.claim: Because a coordinated slowdown lets upstart competitors catch up, the frontier labs' willingness to call for one against their financial interest is evidence their extinction fears are sincere rather than marketing.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Investors should treat lab safety rhetoric as a real policy driver, not hype, implying real risk to growth assumptions.
insights.quote: So the fact that they’re still calling for a slowdown, in defiance of their own financial interests, is a clear sign that their worry about human extinction is sincere.
insights.locator: This is pretty extraordinary.

insights.claim: AI leaders feel trapped in a 'red queen's race' where each believes someone else will build superintelligence anyway, so each races to make sure its own (presumed safest) AI dominates.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Explains why unilateral restraint fails and why only coordinated or regulated slowdowns are plausible.

themes.theme: Bioweapons as the concrete doom path

insights.claim: The most plausible concrete path by which superintelligent AI could kill humanity is bioweapons: AI designing viruses, either at the request of a nihilistic human ordering from a gray-market lab, or by a rogue agent swarm acting on its own.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Biosecurity and lab-access controls are likely regulatory targets alongside AI itself.
insights.quote: The point is that AI can design viruses, and viruses can potentially kill off all or most of humanity.

insights.claim: Biologists' skepticism that AI could design a doomsday virus should be discounted, because domain experts consistently underestimate how fast AI masters their field, mistaking human difficulty for universal difficulty.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Suggests systematically discounting expert pessimism on AI capabilities in any domain.
insights.quote: Domain experts consistently underestimate how quickly AI can master their field and surpass them, because they mistake human difficulties for universal difficulty.

insights.claim: Policy should secure biology labs, police modification of viruses and pathogens, and 'pacing' AI development would also help reduce bio risk.

themes.theme: Scaring China into an AI slowdown

insights.claim: The main objection to pacing is that China would overtake the U.S.; the U.S. is still ahead of China in AI, but only barely, so any U.S. slowdown is futile unless China also slows.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: US-China AI race dynamics remain the binding constraint on any slowdown, sustaining capex momentum absent a deal.
insights.quote: The U.S. is still ahead of China in the AI race, but only just barely.
insights.locator: This is an incredibly reasonable concern.

insights.claim: The author reverses his earlier view that staying ahead of China would persuade it to accept a slowdown, since if China only slows when America doesn't, joint slowdown is impossible.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Shows the leading-edge arms-race logic doesn't produce mutual restraint.
